'''Martha Bailey Briggs''' (March 31, 1838 – March 28, 1889) was an American educator who was born and educated in [[New Bedford, Massachusetts]], where she taught formerly enslaved men and women to read and write.<ref name="nbhs">{{cite web|url=http://nbhistoricalsociety.org/Important-Figures/martha-bailey-briggs/|title=Martha B. Briggs|last1=New Bedford Historical Society|publisher=New Bedford Historical Society}}</ref><ref name="nbaw">{{cite book|last1=Iturralde|first1=Lucilla|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ssMBzqrUpjwC&q=martha+b+briggs&pg=PA55|title=Notable Black American Women, Book 2|last2=Jones|first2=Adrienne|isbn=9780810391772|year=1992|publisher=VNR AG }}</ref> In 1869, she moved to [[Washington, D.C.]], where she taught and served as a principal at Anthony Bowen Elementary School until 1873,<ref name="nbaw" /><ref name=":0" /> when she began work at [[Howard University]].<ref name="nbhs" /> At Howard, she trained teachers and taught math.<ref name="nbhs" /> In 1879, she was hired to serve as principal of the [[Miner Normal School]].<ref name="nbhs"/><ref name="nbaw" /> She stepped down from Miner Normal in 1883 and returned to Howard, where she served as principal of the Howard Normal Department until her death in 1889.<ref name="nbaw" /><ref name=":0" />

==Early life and career==
Martha Bailey Briggs was born March 31, 1838, to John Briggs and Fannie Bassett Briggs, a black abolitionist family in [[New Bedford, Massachusetts]].<ref name="nbwm" /><ref name=":0">Cooke, Paul Phillips. ''Martha Bailey Briggs (1838-1889): A Biographical Treatment Of Her Life With Emphasis On Her Public School Service.'' Prepared for the Charles Sumner School Museum/Archives, Washington, DC, April 1992.</ref> Shortly after his emancipation, [[Frederick Douglass]] worked with John Briggs in New Bedford.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Douglass, Frederick, 1818-1895|title=Autobiographies : Narrative of the life of Frederick Douglass, an American slave; My bondage and my freedom; Life and times of Frederick Douglass|others=Gates, Henry Louis, Jr.|date=February 1994 |isbn=0-940450-79-8|location=New York|oclc=28410345}}</ref> She was the first African American to graduate from her high school.<ref name="wod">{{cite book|url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Women_of_distinction/Chapter_92|title=Women of Distinction: Remarkable in Works and Invincible in Character|last1=Scruggs|first1=Lawson Andrew|chapter=Chapter XCII |year=1893}}</ref> She received teacher education at the [[Bridgewater Normal School]].<ref name=":0" /> Her first teaching experience was in her father's home, tutoring formerly enslaved men and women, many of whom had escaped enslavement through the [[Underground Railroad]]. Her reputation as a teacher grew, and she was also hired to teach in small home-based schools in the region.<ref name="nbhs"/> In addition to teaching at the private school she began, she taught in a private school in Christiantown, [[Martha's Vineyard]], and in public schools of Newport, Rhode Island.<ref name=":0" /> In 1859, [[Myrtilla Miner]] of Washington, D.C., invited Briggs to come to her "School for Colored Girls," but Briggs declined.<ref name=":0" /> Briggs briefly studied nursing at Boston Medical College but did not complete study. Briggs taught in [[Easton, Maryland]], from 1862 to 1869.<ref>[[Charles Sumner School]] Museum & Archives. Martha Bailey Briggs File. Undated newspaper duplications likely to be from the Afro American (Baltimore) circa 1934. Article Titles: "Late Martha Briggs Lauded on Founder's Day at Miner" and "What's Behind the Name of Your School."</ref>

{{Further|Abolitionism in New Bedford, Massachusetts}}

==Career in Washington, DC==
In 1869, Briggs moved to Washington, D.C., where she quickly became both teacher and principal at the Anthony Bowen Elementary School, which permitted children of color to attend.<ref name="wod" /><ref name=":0" /> In 1873, Howard University hired her to teach in their mathematics and teacher preparation programs.<ref name="nbhs" /><ref name="nbaw" /> Following Myrtilla Miner's death, Briggs left Howard to serve as principal of the Miner Normal School (now known as [[University of the District of Columbia]]) from 1879 until 1883.<ref name="arcdc">{{cite book|last1=Board of Commissioners|title=Annual Report of the Commissioners of the District of Columbia|date=1905|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ObdEAQAAMAAJ&q=martha+b+briggs&pg=PA127}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Briggs was the first African American woman to serve as principal of [[Normal School for Colored Girls|Miner Normal]], and a Board of Education Report described her as: "a born teacher, and her work showed those qualities of head and heart that have made her name famous in the annals of education in the character of the graduates."<ref name="wormley">{{cite journal|last1=Wormley|first1=G. Smith|title=Educators of the First Half Century of Public Schools of the District of Columbia|journal=The Journal of Negro History|date=April 1932|volume=17|issue=2|pages=124–140|jstor=2714463|doi=10.2307/2714463|s2cid=149604129}}</ref><ref name="arcdc" /> Briggs was a member of the [[Monday Night Literary Club]], a weekly gathering hosted by [[Frederick Douglass]].

Briggs stepped down from her position with the Miner Normal School to work again for Howard University in 1883, a result of her poor health.<ref name="wod" /><ref name=":0" /> She remained principal of the university's normal department until her death in 1889.<ref name="nbaw" /><ref name="howu">{{cite book|last1=Dyson|first1=Walter|title=Howard University, the capstone of negro education : a history|date=1941|publisher=Howard University|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001450591}}</ref> A personnel roster for Howard lists her degree as [[Doctor of Divinity|D.D.]]<ref name="howu"/> She advocated for vocational as well as liberal arts education for people of color, and was elected president of the Industrial Institute Association of Washington, D.C., shortly before her death.<ref name="wod" />

==Legacy==
After her death on March 28, 1889,<ref name="nbwm">{{cite web|last1=Blake|first1=Lee|title=Martha Bailey Briggs|url=https://www.whalingmuseum.org/explore/partnerships/women-greater-new-bedford/historic-women-profiles-martha-bailey-briggs/|website=New Bedford Whaling Museum}}</ref> a group of citizens, led by [[Frederick Douglass]],<ref name="nbwm"/> successfully petitioned that a DC school building be named the 'Martha B. Briggs Building' after her.<ref name="wod" /><ref name="nbhs" /> Two District of Columbia schools were named after her: Briggs Elementary School in 1889 and Briggs-Montgomery Elementary School; however, both schools were torn down for other construction projects.<ref name=":0" /> A plaque was placed at the Howard University Chapel in her memory, with the inscription: "Her works do follow her."<ref name="wod" /><ref name="nbwm" /> In 1920, a group of educators in New Bedford created the Martha Briggs Educational Club and student aid fund in her honor.<ref name="nbwm" /> In 1935, Briggs' former students  gathered to honor her legacy as part of founders' day celebrations at Miner Teachers College.<ref name="wapofounders">{{cite news|title=Miner Students Honor Founder: Wilkinson Speaks at Rites Held at College.|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=March 10, 1935}}</ref>
